raw_response.headline_result_summary: Using unbalanced panel GEE regressions of 51 Brazilian water and sanitation business corporations from 2005 to 2012 (N = 351 corporation-years for water Lwt and joint Ljt tariffs; N = 349 for sanitation Lst tariffs), Barbosa and Brusca (2015) test three headline governance hypotheses on average tariff levels (R$/m3 billed, where higher values mean higher consumer prices / worse tariff affordability): (1) Private vs. public management (H1): privately managed corporations charge significantly higher joint tariffs (+0.2797 R$/m3, p = 0.026) and water supply tariffs (+0.3456 R$/m3, p = 0.011) than publicly managed corporations in the overall sample, driven by unregulated corporations (+0.3618 R$/m3, p = 0.011), whereas private-public tariff differences are statistically null for sanitation tariffs overall (+0.1971 R$/m3, p = 0.159) and completely null across all three tariff measures among regulated corporations (Lwt p = 0.885, Lst p = 0.259, Ljt p = 0.667); (2) Regulatory agency oversight (H2): corporations regulated by state/micro-regional (RRegA) or municipal/district (LRegA) agencies do not have significantly different tariff levels from unregulated corporations in any model (all p >= 0.518); and (3) Economic regulatory regimes (H3): rate-of-return (Rrat) and price-cap/revenue-cap (Rcap) regimes show no statistically significant difference in tariffs relative to municipal negotiation in the overall models (all p >= 0.191), although within the regulated subsample Rrat significantly raises water (+0.3080 R$/m3, p = 0.015) and joint (+0.2701 R$/m3, p = 0.032) tariffs. Increasing block tariffs (TwoIBT, SinIBT) are associated with higher average tariffs per m3 than uniform volumetric tariffs, while government capital subsidies (Psub) are null overall.
raw_response.specification_or_coding_pitfalls: 1. Outcome polarity trap (price vs. access): The dependent variables (Lwt, Lst, Ljt) are average corporate tariff levels (total annual bills divided by billed m3, in 2012 R$/m3). Positive coefficients indicate HIGHER water/sanitation prices (worse consumer affordability), NOT expanded access or coverage. Moreover, the authors explicitly note (PDF p. 4) that they measure aggregate utility tariff revenue per m3 across all customer classes rather than household connection coverage or income-adjusted household affordability. 2. Stripped Unicode minus signs and p-values in parentheses: In the extracted text of Tables 5-7 (PDF pp. 8-9), Equation (1) (p. 7), and Appendix 1 (pp. 11-12), Elsevier's Unicode minus character was dropped during text extraction, making negative coefficients appear positive unless verified against the prose (e.g., PDF p. 7 states RRegA and LRegA coefficients are negative and non-significant; pp. 9-10 state Psub is negative in the regulated cluster). Also, numbers in parentheses in Tables 5-7 are p-values, NOT standard errors. 3. Multi-hypothesis / family-selection sensitivity: Coding direction depends entirely on which governance exposure a review selects: H1 (private management Priv = 1 vs. public = 0) increases Lwt and Ljt tariffs (unfavorable to affordability, though symmetrical if re-oriented to public ownership, and null for sanitation Lst and regulated utilities), whereas H2 (regulatory agency presence/level) and H3 (rate-of-return or price-cap regime) are statistically null across all overall models. 4. Table 7 printing anomalies in original article: Table 7's header mislabels the Ljt model as 'Lst model', and its Unregulated cluster column (N = 183) prints identical parameter estimates to Table 5's Unregulated cluster column for shared variables.
raw_response.study_design: Longitudinal / unbalanced panel observational econometric study (2005-2012) using Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE) with Gaussian family, identity link, independent working correlation matrix, and robust standard errors
raw_response.unit_and_sample_size: Unit of analysis: Brazilian water and sanitation utility (WSU) business corporations observed annually (2005-2012). Sample: 51 out of 52 corporate WSUs in Brazil (covering ~73% of national water supply population and ~74% of sanitation services), yielding N = 351 corporation-year observations for water supply (Lwt) and joint (Ljt) tariff models (Regulated cluster N = 168; Unregulated cluster N = 183) and N = 349 observations for the sanitation (Lst) tariff model after removing 2 outliers (Regulated cluster N = 167; Unregulated cluster N = 182).
